data.title: Ladce, Tunežice and Nozdrovice – one hillfort of the Púchov culture
data.excerpt: The site called Hradište extends into the cadastral areas of Nozdrovice and Tunežice and is sometimes listed as Ladce or Košeca, yet it is a single hillfort, known for a very long time. Since the 1930s sherds of Púchov culture vessels have been found here; the adjacent settlement is one of the largest of the culture in north-western Slovakia, and a hoard with 10 to 12 Celtic coins of the Divinka type comes from the hillfort itself.
data.metaTitle: Ladce–Tunežice: one hillfort of the Púchov culture
data.metaDescription: One hillfort shared by Nozdrovice, Tunežice and Ladce, known since the 1930s for the Púchov culture finds that reached V. Budinský-Krička in Martin.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: The hillfort lies in the cadastral areas of Nozdrovice and Tunežice; it is sometimes listed also as Ladce or Košeca

keyFacts.label: Size of the settlement
keyFacts.value: The adjacent settlement is one of the largest settlements of the Púchov culture in north-western Slovakia

keyFacts.label: Hoard of Celtic coins
keyFacts.value: A hoard with 10 to 12 coins of the Divinka type was found on the hillfort – the largest known number of this type so far

keyFacts.label: A unique little vessel
keyFacts.value: A complete, undamaged small vessel decorated with a band of leaves of varying size at the mouth of the pot was found – a find without parallel

keyFacts.label: Source of the bitumen on the pottery
keyFacts.value: The pitch coating on a storage vessel came from the single known source of natural bitumen in Central Europe, at Nezbudská Lúčka near Varín

keyFacts.label: A coin of the Eravisci
keyFacts.value: The find of a coin of the Eravisci, a tribe of Pannonian Celts, is entirely unique on hillforts of the Púchov culture

keyFacts.label: End of the occupation
keyFacts.value: Both the settlement and the hillfort came to an end during the invasion of the Germanic peoples at the turn of the era

keyFacts.label: Sources
keyFacts.value: The basic source is the monograph Lipták B. et al.: Ladce (Ametyst, 2003)

timeline.title: First finds of Púchov culture pottery
timeline.description: Sherds of Púchov culture vessels began to be found on the hillfort; some of them reached the Slovak National Museum in Martin and Professor Vojtech Budinský-Krička.

timeline.title: Duration of the settlement beside the hillfort
timeline.description: The settlement on the western, south-western and south-eastern side of the defences lasted at least throughout the 1st century BC and into the first decades of the new era.

timeline.title: Destruction of the hillfort by the Germanic peoples
timeline.description: The hillfort, together with the adjacent settlement, was destroyed during the invasion of the Germanic peoples, who caused the interruption of the development of the Púchov culture at the time of its greatest flowering.

timeline.year: 2nd half of the 1st c. AD – end of the 2nd c. AD
timeline.title: Shrinking of the Púchov culture territory
timeline.description: The territory occupied by the Púchov culture shrank significantly, the number of archaeological sites fell to roughly a quarter, and only some of the hillforts were still used.

timeline.year: turn of the 2nd and 3rd c. AD
timeline.title: Dating of the Germanic settlement at Beluša
timeline.description: On the basis of bronze brooches, the Germanic, Quadic settlement discovered at Beluša (the locality known as Pechová) was placed at the turn of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD.

timeline.title: Demise of the Púchov culture
timeline.description: After the Cotini had been carried off to Pannonia during the Marcomannic Wars, the Púchov culture came to an end and Germanic peoples from the west began to penetrate the emptied space.

timeline.title: The campaign of the legions of Marcus Aurelius
timeline.description: After the victorious battles of the Roman legions, the emperor Marcus Aurelius ordered the occupation of the Carpathian passes in order to prevent the Quadi from fleeing northwards to their kinsmen.

timeline.title: The earliest Slavic finds around Ladce
timeline.description: In the immediate surroundings of Ladce the earliest Slavic finds attested so far are from the 8th and 9th centuries; the neighbouring cadastral area of Beluša is strewn with Slavic barrow cemeteries.

timeline.title: Excavation of the Slavic barrow cemeteries at Beluša
timeline.description: Up to 85 barrows were identified at seven places; the excavations in the localities known as Koscelisče and Garové produced finds of weapons including a Great Moravian bearded axe.

timeline.title: Dating of the iron spearhead from Ladce
timeline.description: According to the chronology worked out by Prof. A. Rutkay, the iron spearhead found in the riverbed of the Váh may come from the period of the Slavic occupation, specifically from the time horizon of the 9th to the 11th century.

timeline.title: Discovery of Late Hillfort-period occupation
timeline.description: In his key article Petrovský-Šichman reported that Š. Križanová had found Late Hillfort-period occupation at the foot of Hradište, which suggests that the hillfort was used by the Slavs as a place of refuge.

timeline.title: Striking of the coins of the Divinka type
timeline.description: Following the model of the Prague quinarii, coins of the Divinka type began to be struck on one of the hillforts of the Púchov culture in the middle Váh region, probably at Divinka.

timeline.title: Find of a Roman republican coin from Nozdrovice
timeline.description: The later Roman republican coin found at Nozdrovice comes from approximately the year 48 BC and confirms the dating of the coins of the Divinka type to the third quarter of the 1st century BC.

children.text: The site called Hradište at Nozdrovice extends into the cadastral area of Tunežice as well, and is sometimes listed also as Ladce or Košeca, yet it is still a single hillfort, one that has been known for a very long time. Since the 1930s sherds of Púchov culture vessels have been found here, some of which reached the Slovak National Museum in Martin and Professor Vojtech Budinský-Krička (who at that time used the name Budaváry). Repeated surveys of these defences by Šarlota Križanová again yielded rich finds of Púchov culture pottery. She found them in several places, at a depth of 90 cm in a thick occupation layer mixed with sherds and animal bones. The sherds came mainly from vessels with a rough surface, handmade and decorated with vertical grooves, so-called combing. However, fragments of very fine wheel-thrown pottery were also found, as well as sherds from graphite vessels and one broken pyramidal clay loom weight.

children.text: Spindle whorls (the flywheels of spindles) and loom weights are evidence of textile working and of the production of cloth on simple looms of the kind that it proved possible to reconstruct during the excavation at Liptovská Mara. A replica of such a loom can also be seen in the Púchov culture exhibition in Púchov. While the spindle whorls were used on the end of the spindle onto which the spun yarn was wound, the clay weights served to tension the warp on the loom so that the woven cloth would be firm.

Later excavation of Hradište at Nozdrovice and its immediate surroundings also produced further vessel fragments, in particular the distinctive rims of graphite situlae, sherds of graphite vessels decorated with combing, sherds from large bowls with inturned rims, sherds decorated with a plastic crescent-shaped ornament and others. The settlement situated on the western, south-western and south-eastern side of the defences is one of the largest settlements of the Púchov culture in north-western Slovakia. It evidently had a long duration, lasting at least throughout the 1st century BC and into the first decades of the new era, when it was destroyed together with the hillfort during the invasion of the Germanic peoples. It was precisely the Germanic peoples who caused the interruption of the development of the Púchov culture at the time of its greatest flowering. Already in the 2nd half of the 1st century AD and up to the end of the 2nd century the territory of the Púchov culture shrank significantly. The number of archaeological sites of this period compared with the preceding one was in a ratio of about 1:4. Of the hillforts only some were still used, above all Púchovská Skala and other smaller defended sites, where it also proved possible to discover remains from the Early Roman period. Among the smaller settlements that may have survived the Germanic invasion we can perhaps also count the site at Hlože by the quarry (the second one from Beluša), in the valley leading to Mojtín. Besides the usual Púchov culture sherds from graphite vessels and bowls with inturned rims, there were also fragments of wheel-thrown vessels here and parts of clay storage vessels with a broad flat rim collar.

A unique find, however, was an entirely complete small barrel-shaped vessel, handmade and decorated with an exceptional ornament in the form of a band of leaves of varying size at the mouth of the pot. This find has so far no parallel in the territory of present-day Slovakia, and it may perhaps therefore be regarded as an exceptional object serving for cult rites. It is also particularly remarkable that the little vessel was found whole and undamaged, which is not usual on settlements of the Púchov culture. Another peculiarity is a pitch coating on the outer wall of a sherd of a large storage vessel, which served not only for decoration but above all for greater impermeability, in case liquid food was kept in the storage vessel. This way of treating the surface of vessels appears quite often in the environment of the Púchov culture, and it seems that what is involved here is the use of the single source of natural bitumen in Central Europe, which lay at Nezbudská Lúčka near Varín (Žilina district), but which was completely worked out in the 1920s and 1930s. Now there is only a deep lake there (20 m) with clean but very cold water. The pitch coating occurs frequently, and so it was probably already in use in the Late Iron Age.

It seems that the demise of the Púchov culture at the end of the 2nd century AD, after the Cotini had been carried off to Pannonia, is confirmed also by the penetration of the Germanic peoples from south-western Slovakia northwards into the emptied space. Evidence of this is also the Germanic, Quadic settlement discovered at Beluša, in the locality known as Pechová, where not only Germanic dwellings were investigated but also a pottery kiln. On the basis of well datable finds (above all bronze brooches) the settlement is placed at the turn of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD.

Another example of the penetration of the Germanic peoples into north-western Slovakia is a cremation grave at Ilava, in which there was found a biconical little vessel decorated with pronounced grooves, part of a large storage vessel decorated with dense wavy lines, and also an iron winged spearhead, an iron spear-butt (the fitting of the lower part of the spear shaft) and a large iron ring. It is therefore not particularly surprising that the iron dagger of a Roman officer, called a pugio, from Tuchyňa was also found so deep in the Barbaricum. It is evidently evidence of the movement of the Roman legions as far as this region, whether in connection with the above-mentioned transfer of the Cotini to Pannonia, or in connection with the occupation of the Carpathian passes ordered by the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius after the victorious battles of the legions at the turn of the years 179 to 180, in order to prevent the Quadi from fleeing northwards to their kinsmen.

Occupation of further periods is attested only very late here, even though on the other side of the Váh there are settlements from the Late Roman period and from the Migration Period (5th and 6th centuries AD) as well. In the immediate surroundings of Ladce the earliest Slavic finds attested so far are from the 8th and 9th centuries. Above all the territory of the neighbouring cadastral area of Beluša is literally strewn with Slavic barrow cemeteries, where, especially in the 1950s and 1960s, up to 85 barrows were identified at seven places. Excavations in the localities known as Koscelisče (34 barrows) and Garové (25 barrows) also produced finds of the weapons that Slavic warriors used in the defence of this territory. This is the well-known Great Moravian bearded axe, which has, beside the opening for the shaft, also tall spikes, barbs, for better fixing of the axe to the haft. The investigated graves also contained fragments of iron knives and, of course, sherds from broken vessels. From the territory of Ladce itself only a single iron spearhead comes, which was found in the riverbed of the Váh. It is kept in the collections of the Slovak National Museum in Martin. According to the chronology worked out by Prof. A. Rutkay, DrSc., however, it may come from the period of the Slavic occupation of this territory, its period of use falling within the time horizon from the 9th to the 11th century. The overall length of the spearhead is 23 cm; it has a narrow blade and a longer socket for the insertion of the shaft. Among the Púchov culture sherds obtained from the quarry in the cadastral area of Hlože there also appeared a fragment of a Slavic vessel decorated with horizontal bundles of fine grooves, which on the basis of this decorative element we can date to the 9th century. It is therefore evidently only a matter of time before more convincing evidence of occupation of the cadastral area of Ladce in the Slavic period as well is found.

The most important contribution to our knowledge and above all to the extension of the territory in which coins of the Divinka type were used is the hoard found by treasure hunters on Hradište near Nozdrovice. It contained several types of coins, among which there were also 10 or 12 pieces of the Divinka type. Besides these, two tetradrachms of the Veľký Bysterec type also appeared here, of high weight and in good-quality striking. The finds well represent the coinage of the north Slovak cultural environment in the 1st century BC. Similar coins have already been found at several sites of the Púchov culture, and one of the specimens found on Hradište near Nozdrovice even has on its obverse a hint of the inscription CA, which occurs rarely as CAT on certain other finds. CAT is explained as an abbreviation of the name of the Cotini, who are regarded as the principal representatives of the Púchov culture. With their migration to Pannonia at the end of the 2nd century AD, during the Marcomannic Wars, the Púchov culture itself came to an end.

Until recently tetradrachms of the Velem type did not occur in Slovakia at all. Apart from the find from Hradište, two similar specimens have recently appeared on the hillfort at Trenčianske Bohuslavice and one at Hubina, Piešťany district, likewise in the locality known as Hradište. These finds speak of important contacts between north-western Slovakia and the Celtic hillfort at Velemszentvid in north-western Hungary in the 2nd half of the 2nd century BC. A small silver coin with an image resembling a shell is so far the only one of its kind among the finds from the territory of present-day Slovakia. A similar find, though not identical, comes from the Czech oppidum at Stradonice. It is possible that the coin found on Hradište near Nozdrovice also comes from the environment of the Celtic Boii, who occupied a large territory of what is now the Czech Republic and, in the end, in all probability gave their name to the region of Bojohemum — Bohemia. There they built massive hillforts which, after G. I. Caesar's term for them, came to be called oppida.

An entirely unique find on hillforts of the Púchov culture, however, is a coin of the Eravisci, a Pannonian tribe of the Celts who lived in the Late La Tène period and at the beginning of the Early Roman period in the area of the bend of the Danube. They struck their coins probably in their tribal seat in the locality known as Tabán, in the territory of present-day Budapest, at the end of the 2nd half of the 1st century BC. Already before 1870 a whole hoard of these coins was found at Rajecká Lesná near the hamlet of Trstená, but unfortunately it was lost during the war in the Moravian Provincial Museum in Brno, where it had originally been deposited. The coins clearly bear the struck inscription RAVIT - RAVIS, which is in fact an abbreviation of the name of the Eravisci.

As has already been mentioned, the most important assemblage from the hoard on Hradište near Nozdrovice is the 10 to 12 coins of the Divinka type. This is evidently the largest number of these coins so far, although we cannot say whether similar ones were not found during other activities of treasure hunters. For example at Udiča in the locality known as Klape, or at Žilina-Vraňa on the defended site of Rochovica, from where we have positive knowledge that Celtic coins were found here but went abroad and ended up in private hands. Coins of the Divinka type are very similar to the so-called Prague quinarii, which were struck in the middle of the 1st century BC and whose finds are concentrated above all in the territory of Prague or on the great Celtic oppidum at Stradonice. They are also represented in the territory of Germany. These, however, do not have such a stylised image as the Divinka type has. The head on the obverse and the horse on the reverse are still quite distinct. Their possible models are considered to be imitations of Roman republican denarii of the Roma/horse type, which were struck in the territory of Gaul (present-day France) probably in the middle of the 1st century BC. If we assume that coins of the Divinka type were struck after the model of the Prague quinarii, with a certain time lag, on some of the hillforts of the Púchov culture in the middle Váh region (probably first of all on the hillfort at Divinka, which was at that time the largest central defended site), the period between 45 and 35 BC could come into consideration. This dating is also indicated by the find of a later Roman republican coin from Nozdrovice, which comes from approximately the year 48 BC. This in fact also confirms the assumption that coins of the Divinka type were struck at the earliest in the third quarter of the 1st century BC. They were used in the territory of the tribe which had its central hillfort on Veľký vrch at Divinka, since finds of this type of Celtic coin are so far not known from a single one of the regions occupied by the people of the Púchov culture (Liptov, Orava, Turiec, Spiš). They therefore probably speak above all of intensive contacts between the local population and the western Celtic world, which at the same time may have been decisive for the economic development of Ladce and its surroundings as well.

To Mr Moravčík's article I would add that in his key article of 1964 Petrovský-Šichman mentions that Š. Križanová found Late Hillfort-period occupation at the foot of Hradište, which evidently leads to the consideration that the hillfort was used by the Slavs as well, at least as a place of refuge.
